resources.title: Elements of music
resources.summary: The musical elements the exam describes every piece through, each with Pearson's own definition and the words from the specification's vocabulary list to use for it.

blocks.title: Seven elements
rows: "how high or low sounds are", in the melody and the harmony
melody, conjunct, disjunct, leap, sequence, ostinato, riff, pedal, drone, chord, cadence, dissonance
"the relationship of notes within a scale or mode to a principal note"
major, minor, modal, pentatonic, chromatic, atonal, modulation, relative minor
binary, ternary, rondo, strophic, through-composed, sonata form, introduction, phrase
"the nature and quality of musical sounds"
timbre, articulation, legato, staccato, pizzicato, glissando, harmonics
"the number of parts in a piece of music and how they relate to one another"
monophony, homophony, polyphony, heterophony, imitation, accompaniment, continuo
the speed, the pattern of strong and weak beats, and how sounds relate to time
beat, dotted rhythm, syncopation, swung rhythm, shuffle, triplets
accent, and the symbols such as *f* and *p*
blocks.note: The quotations are from the specification's vocabulary list, which also defines every word in the third column. Structure is the spec's *form*, and sonority covers *timbre*.

blocks.body: **Use them to plan an answer.** Asked to describe a passage, go through the elements in turn and give one precise word for each, with where it happens: *the melody is conjunct at first, then leaps up an octave; the texture is homophonic; the tonality is minor.*

applications.title: Talking about any song
applications.body: The same seven headings describe a pop song as well as a concerto: a riff in the bass is organisation of pitch, a sudden drop to one voice is texture, a key change for the last chorus is tonality.

applications.title: Film music
applications.body: Composers change one element at a time to change a scene's mood: slow the tempo, drop to a minor key, or thin the texture to a single instrument.

resources.title: Set works at a glance
resources.summary: The eight set works on one page: the area of study each belongs to, who wrote it, and the kind of score the exam uses, with a link to the topic that teaches it.

sources.name: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Music set works information

blocks.title: Eight set works, four areas of study
rows: Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 in D, 3rd movement
Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor ("Pathétique"), 1st movement
short score: vocals, piano, guitars, drums
Main Title / Rebel Blockade Runner, from *Star Wars: Episode IV*
short score: orchestra on two staves
James McNally, Iarla Ó Lionáird, Russell Martin, Sinéad O'Connor and Simon Emmerson (Afro Celt Sound System)
Vinicius de Moraes and Baden Powell de Aquino

blocks.note: Section A of the exam asks about six of the eight. Pearson names a recording of each in its set works information; listen to that recording, with the score, as you revise.

applications.title: Comparing across centuries
applications.body: Section B pairs a set work with a piece you have not heard from the same area of study, so knowing Bach and Beethoven well is how you describe an unfamiliar Mozart or Haydn.

applications.title: A playlist for revision
applications.body: Eight pieces, from a Baroque concerto to a Brazilian samba, make one revision playlist. Listening while following the score is revision in itself.

resources.title: Note values and rests
resources.summary: Every note and rest from the semibreve to the semiquaver, how many crotchet beats each lasts, and what a dot and a triplet do.
resources.statusNote: The vocabulary list leaves out note names "(crotchet, minim, etc.)" because the exam assumes you know them, so learn them.

blocks.title: Notes and rests
blocks.note: Each rest lasts as long as the note of the same name. In $\tfrac{4}{4}$ time a bar holds four crotchet beats: one semibreve, two minims, or eight quavers.

blocks.body:
**A dot** adds half the note's value again: a dotted minim is $2 + 1 = 3$ beats, a dotted crotchet $1 + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\tfrac{1}{2}$.

**A triplet** squeezes three notes into the time of two: three triplet quavers take one crotchet beat.

**A dotted rhythm** pairs a dotted note with a short one, such as a dotted quaver and a semiquaver, giving a jagged, jumpy feel.

applications.title: Reading a drum part
applications.body: A rock drummer's hi-hat often plays steady quavers, eight to a bar of $\tfrac{4}{4}$, while the bass drum plays crotchets on the beat.

applications.title: Rhythmic dictation
applications.body: The dictation question asks you to fill in missing rhythms. Counting the beats left in the bar tells you which note values can fit.

resources.title: Instruments of the orchestra
resources.summary: The four families of the orchestra, the instruments in each, how they make their sound and where they sit, and beyond the orchestra: keyboards, band instruments and voice types.

blocks.title: The orchestra
rows: violin, viola, cello, double bass; the harp
at the front, nearest the conductor
blowing across a hole, or through a single or double reed
behind the strings, in the middle
buzzing the lips into a mouthpiece
timpani, snare drum, bass drum, cymbals, xylophone, glockenspiel
blocks.note: The higher an instrument in its family, the smaller it is: the violin is the smallest string instrument and the highest, the double bass the largest and lowest.

blocks.title: Beyond the orchestra
rows: electric guitar, bass guitar, drum kit, keyboards
blocks.note: The specification expects you to recognise the sound of all of these; most can be heard in the eight set works.

applications.title: Film scores
applications.body: A film composer picks a family for a feeling: brass for heroism, as in the *Star Wars* main title, strings for tension or romance, woodwind for something light or pastoral.

applications.title: Baroque bands
applications.body: Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 uses a harpsichord, a keyboard, as a soloist alongside flute and violin, with strings accompanying: an orchestra before the modern one existed.
